title: Jesus Sat at Their Tables—and Still Called Them Out of the Darkness
paragraphs: Jesus Sat at Their Tables—and Still Called Them Out of the Darkness

How Jesus responded to sexual sinners reveals something far more unsettling than condemnation—and far more costly than permission. He offered a grace that refused to abandon people either to their shame or to their sin.
There is a kind of sin Christians sometimes whisper about differently.
We can talk about pride.
We can admit anger.
We can confess anxiety, greed, bitterness, jealousy, even addiction in carefully chosen words.
But sexual sin?
That one changes the temperature in the room.
A secret affair.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Sex outside marriage that became normal because everybody else calls it normal.
A marriage bed betrayed.
A body sold.
A relationship Scripture will not bless.
Desire nurtured until it became a hidden master.
Memories you wish you could erase.
Things done to you that were never yours to be ashamed of.
Things done by you that you cannot undo.
Suddenly, people stop talking.
Because sexual brokenness reaches somewhere painfully personal.
And perhaps that is why one question matters so much:
What did Jesus actually do when sexually broken and sexually sinful people came near Him?
Not what modern outrage culture does.
Not what permissive culture does.
Not what religious hypocrisy sometimes does.
What did Jesus do?
The answer is uncomfortable for almost everyone.
Because Jesus was more compassionate than the self-righteous wanted Him to be...
and far more serious about sin than the permissive wanted Him to be.
That tension is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not look at sexual sinners and say, “You are too filthy for Me.”
But neither did He say, “Nothing needs to change.”
He came with something infinitely better:
grace that receives the sinner and holiness that transforms the sinner.
Look at the woman at the well.
John 4 does not introduce us to a polished religious woman. Jesus meets a Samaritan woman carrying a complicated relational history.
He asks her to call her husband.
She answers:
“I have no husband.”
And Jesus responds that she has spoken truthfully. She has had five husbands, and the man she presently has is not her husband.
Notice what Jesus does not do.
He does not pretend her situation is something it is not.
He names reality.
Yet He does not humiliate her.
He already knew her history before He started the conversation.
Read that again.
Jesus knew before He stayed.
He knew the relationships.
He knew the wounds.
He knew the choices.
He knew the history she could not rewrite.
And He still spoke to her.

In a world where Jewish-Samaritan hostility was real and where this conversation crossed significant social boundaries, Jesus deliberately engaged her and began revealing something astonishing: the Messiah she needed was standing in front of her.
Eventually Jesus tells her:
“I who speak to you am he.” — John 4:26
The Greek is striking:
Ἐγώ εἰμι, ὁ λαλῶν σοι — Egō eimi, ho lalōn soi.
“I am [He], the One speaking to you.”
The woman with the complicated past becomes one of the people in John's Gospel to whom Jesus explicitly identifies Himself as Messiah.
Her history did not make Jesus retreat.
But His kindness did not require Him to rewrite the truth about her life either.
That is Christlike grace.
Grace does not need a lie in order to be compassionate.
And truth does not need cruelty in order to remain true.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
Maybe you have assumed there are only two possibilities.
Either God condemns you and wants nothing to do with you...
or God accepts you by pretending your sin does not matter.
But the Gospel gives us a third reality:
Jesus loves sinners enough to come near, and loves them too much to leave sin enthroned.
That is why Christ's response to sexual sin cannot honestly be reduced to either “condemn everybody” or “affirm everything.”
Jesus does neither.
He calls sinners to Himself.
And when sinners come to Him, repentance is not the price they pay to purchase His mercy.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has encountered the King.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance.
A change of mind and heart resulting in a changed direction.
Not merely feeling disgusting.
Not self-hatred.
Not public humiliation.
Not promising God you will become perfect overnight.
It is turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning toward God.
And sometimes that turning happens while tears are still falling.
Luke 7 gives us another unforgettable scene.
Jesus is eating in the home of Simon, a Pharisee, when a woman known in the city as a sinner enters.

Luke does not explicitly identify her sin as sexual, so we should not claim more than Scripture tells us. Historically, many interpreters have associated her reputation with sexual immorality, but the text itself simply calls her ἁμαρτωλός — hamartōlos, “sinful” or “a sinner.”
She comes behind Jesus weeping.
Her tears fall onto His feet.
She wipes them with her hair.
She kisses His feet.
She anoints them with perfume.
Imagine the room.
Imagine the staring.
Imagine Simon's internal reaction.
Luke tells us what he thinks:
If Jesus were truly a prophet, surely He would know what kind of woman was touching Him.
But that is exactly the point.
Jesus does know.
He knows who is touching Him.
And He does not recoil.
Simon sees contamination.
Jesus sees a human being.
Simon sees a reputation.
Jesus sees repentance, love, and faith.
Then Jesus says words that must have sounded impossible to someone accustomed to being reduced to her past:
“Your sins are forgiven.” — Luke 7:48
In Greek:
Ἀφέωνταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι — Apheōntai sou hai hamartiai.
“Your sins have been forgiven.”
Not hidden.
Forgiven.
Not renamed.
Forgiven.
Not declared harmless.
Forgiven.
Christianity does not proclaim that sin was never serious.
Christianity proclaims something far more magnificent:
sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross, and God's grace is so great that the repentant sinner can be forgiven.
This is where some of us have misunderstood Jesus.
We imagine holiness as Jesus standing at a safe distance from dirty people.
But the Gospels show the Holy One walking straight toward them.
Eating with sinners.
Speaking with the rejected.
Touching the unclean.
Receiving the ashamed.
And eventually carrying sin to a Roman cross.
Yet His nearness should never be mistaken for moral indifference.

Jesus Himself taught that sexual immorality comes from the human heart and defiles a person (Matthew 15:19–20). He reaffirmed God's creational design for marriage by pointing back to Genesis: male and female, joined as husband and wife, becoming one flesh (Matthew 19:4–6).
Jesus was not embarrassed by biblical sexual holiness.
Neither was He eager to weaponize holiness against wounded people.
That combination is rare.
Truth without compassion can become brutality.
Compassion detached from truth can become permission.
Jesus embodies “grace and truth” (John 1:14).
Not fifty percent grace and fifty percent truth.
He is full of both.
And perhaps nowhere is the scandal of grace more visible than at the cross.
Because eventually the question stops being:
“How did Jesus respond to those sexual sinners?”
And becomes:
How does Jesus respond to me?
That is harder.
Because “sexual sinners” are easier to discuss when they are somewhere else.
Someone on the news.
Someone in another church.
Someone with a scandal.
Someone whose lifestyle makes us uncomfortable.
Someone whose marriage collapsed publicly.
Someone whose browser history became known.
Someone whose pregnancy exposed what had been hidden.
Someone caught cheating.
Someone selling their body.
Someone consuming bodies through a screen.
Someone whose desires and relationships conflict with biblical teaching.
Someone whose past follows them into every church they enter.
But Scripture will not allow us to stand safely outside the category of sinners.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The Greek says:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον — pantes gar hēmarton.
“For all sinned.”
All.
That word dismantles the pedestal.
The pornography user cannot throw stones at the adulterer.
The adulterer cannot look down on the prostitute.
The sexually disciplined Christian cannot boast before God as though self-control purchased salvation.
And the person whose sexual sins are visible is not automatically more guilty before God than the religious person whose pride, hatred, greed, hypocrisy, or lust remains carefully concealed.
Jesus made this terrifyingly personal in the Sermon on the Mount.
He did not allow people to congratulate themselves merely because adultery had not become physical.
He said that looking with lustful intent is already adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28).
Suddenly the courtroom becomes very quiet.
Because Jesus moves the discussion from beds...
to hearts.
From scandal...
to desire.
From reputation...
to reality.
And now perhaps the person holding the stone realizes he needs mercy too.
There is a famous Gospel scene often brought into this conversation: the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11.
We should handle it carefully.

Many modern Bibles note that the earliest manuscripts do not contain this passage, and responsible Christian teaching should acknowledge that textual issue rather than hiding it. The account has a long history in the Christian tradition and beautifully portrays themes consistent with Jesus' ministry, but major doctrine should not depend upon this disputed passage alone.
With that qualification understood, its famous conclusion captures the tension we see throughout the undisputed Gospel witness.
Jesus refuses condemnation from hypocritical accusers, then tells the woman to leave her life of sin.
Mercy...
and transformation.
Neither cheap condemnation nor cheap grace.
That pattern is unquestionably supported elsewhere in the New Testament.
And it leads directly to the cross.
Jesus did not die because human beings merely needed improved self-esteem.
He died because we needed reconciliation with God.
Paul writes:
While we were still sinners.
Not after the pornography addiction disappeared.
Not after the affair had been repaired.
Not after every disordered desire vanished.
Not after you had cleaned yourself enough to approach God.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means mercy comes from Christ, not from our ability to make ourselves worthy of mercy.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps nobody knows what you did.
Perhaps everybody knows.
Perhaps you have confessed it to God a hundred times and still wake up feeling dirty.
Perhaps you keep returning to the same screen.
Perhaps you promised your spouse it was over.
Perhaps you promised Jesus it was over.
Perhaps you meant it.
Then you fell again.
And now shame is whispering something that sounds spiritual but is actually driving you farther from Christ:
“Don't come back until you're better.”
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel says come to Christ because you cannot save yourself.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without excuses.
Come without rewriting Scripture to protect your desires.
Come without pretending temptation itself makes you uniquely disgusting.
Come without hiding the sin you chose.
Come without carrying shame for abuse committed against you—as though another person's evil made you guilty.
Come because Jesus Christ still receives sinners.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the floor.
Get up and run toward Him again.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly drags you into sin.
Tell the truth where restitution and confession are biblically appropriate.
Seek wise pastoral help and, when needed, qualified professional support.
Do not call bondage freedom simply because surrender hurts.
There is something better than hiding.
There is forgiveness.
John writes:
The word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō: to confess, acknowledge, agree.
There is something beautiful about that.
Confession stops negotiating with God about what God already sees.
You finally stop defending.
Stop editing.
Stop pretending.
You bring the real thing into the light.
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“This is what I keep wanting.”
“This is where I betrayed You.”
“This is where I betrayed someone who trusted me.”
“This is where I am enslaved.”
“This is where I need mercy.”
And the Gospel does not answer the repentant sinner with a locked door.
It answers with a wounded Savior.
Hands pierced.
Blood poured out.
A cross occupied.
A tomb emptied.
A King alive.
The Christian answer to sexual brokenness is ultimately not “try harder.”
It is Jesus Christ crucified and risen, calling sinners into union with Him and a new way of life.
Paul could write to Christians in Corinth after listing serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality and adultery:
“And such were some of you.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11
Were.
That tiny word carries thunder.
Not because every temptation instantly disappeared.
Not because Christians became incapable of falling.
But because sin no longer possessed the right to define their identity or rule their lives.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That is what scandal looks like after grace gets hold of it.
Your worst sexual sin does not become good.
Something far greater happens.
Jesus can redeem the sinner.
The Gospel does not rewrite God's definition of sin.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's story.
That is the difference.
And maybe this article found you at an hour when nobody knows what is happening inside you.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe your secret is growing.
Maybe shame has made church unbearable.
Maybe religious people wounded you so deeply that you assumed Jesus must despise you too.
Maybe you have been using “grace” as permission because surrender frightens you.
Maybe you have been using “truth” as a weapon because condemning someone else's sexual sin keeps you from confronting your own heart.
Either way, Jesus is calling us out of hiding.
Not into humiliation.
Into light.
If this exposed something hidden in you, you do not need to tell strangers the details. But you can make one small declaration that shame does not get the final word.
Somebody reading beneath you may need to discover that Christians are not people with spotless histories.
We are people who desperately need a spotless Savior.
Not because an article can rescue you, but because there may come another night when shame starts preaching again and you need to remember what Scripture actually says.
Do it gently.
Never weaponize this article by publicly tagging someone in a way that exposes their private struggle.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him.
But before you leave, remember the woman at the well.
Jesus knew.
Before the conversation began...
He knew.
Before she admitted anything...
He knew.
And He stayed.
The same Christ who knows the chapter you desperately wish could be torn from your story is the Christ who went to the cross for sinners.
Repentance does not mean your story is over.
In Christ, it may mean you have finally stopped letting your darkest chapter write the ending.
Because when Jesus saves a sinner, He does not merely cover a scandal with religious language.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He calls.
He restores.
He transforms.
And He teaches redeemed people to walk in the light.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but at the feet of Jesus, it does not get to decide where grace will take you.
